10472-arthurian-chronicles-roman-de-brut:
Wace, a Norman poet, wrote the Roman de Brut in verse, translated here by Eugene Mason. The chronicle follows Geoffrey of Monmouth, whose Historia Regum Britanniae first united scattered Arthur legends into a lasting history. Wace, writing after Geoffrey, gave the story French verse form and wide fame.

About 1150, Geoffrey Gaimar had tried a French metrical chronicle, but Wace's Brut cast it into shade. Wace's gifts as poet and storyteller shaped Arthur's place in later annals. Readers get a key Arthurian source, in clear prose, for students of legend and medieval literature.
10856-a-narrative-of-the-siege-of-delhi-:
Charles John Griffiths, late captain of the 61st Regiment, wrote A Narrative of the Siege of Delhi. Henry John Yonge edited it, and John Murray published it in 1910, with plans and illustrations. The book opens at Ferozepore from May 10 to June 13, 1857: outbreak at Meerut, neglected arsenals, disaffection, and the 45th Native Infantry's failed attempt on the fort. Wives and families move to barracks as the cantonment burns.

Griffiths then follows the regiment to Delhi and the siege itself, from a soldier's view. His account criticizes commanders, praises troops, and records the mutiny's first shocks. Readers get a firsthand British narrative of 1857, detailed and partisan, as its officers remembered it.
11561-people-of-the-whirlpool-from-the-e:
Mabel Osgood Wright's 1903 novel is told from the experience book of a commuter's wife, opening on Candlemas with twins, a garden book, and a mild grey day. Letters from Miss Lavinia and Martin Cortright, a trip to town, and February violets follow in the early chapters.

As the whirl begins, families rearrange, gossip spreads, and a bug hunter joins the social round. The narrator's garden, her boys, and her neighbours give the book its shape, and the whirlpool of the title is the busy, talkative world just outside a suburban home.
14305-layamon-s-brut:
Layamon's Brut retells the chronicle of Britain's kings in vigorous early English verse, here in a readable modern rendering. Constantin the fair lands at Totnes with two thousand knights, summons brave men across the kingdom, and marches on London. Britons hiding in pits, woods, and fens like badgers pour out at his coming, women in men's clothes among them, thousands strong.

Arthur dominates the later narrative. Uther musters seven thousand chosen knights before, seven thousand thanes in the middle, and eighteen thousand behind, with footmen beyond counting, then marches to Meneve. Gillomar's men seize spears and battle-axes, breeches off, strange to see. Arthur demands peace with wisdom, reconciles the Danish king and his eldest son, and musters hosts from Norway, Denmark, Orkney, Moray, Galloway, Ireland, and Britain for France. Chronicle, legend, and battle poetry merge in a foundation text of English story.
144-the-voyage-out:
Rachel Vinrace sails to South America with her father and aunt, seeking a life beyond London drawing rooms. Virginia Woolf's Voyage Out, her first novel, follows Rachel among shipboard guests, a hotel colony, and a young writer named Terence Hewet. Talk, walks, and illness shape her growth.

Woolf experiments with free thought and shifting views while keeping a clear story line. Rachel's engagement to Terence promises a new life, but fever cuts it short. The novel's ending, quiet and stark, surprised early readers. It shows Woolf's voice forming before her great experiments.
14408-manners-and-conduct-in-school-and-:
The deans of girls in Chicago high schools wrote this 1921 guide to manners and conduct. It opens with maxims from Lincoln, Franklin, and Disraeli, and a verse from Spenser on gentle deeds. The book then gives plain rules for halls, classrooms, and streets. It speaks to schoolgirls who must learn how to behave in company. Its tone is firm, kindly, and old-fashioned.

In the assembly hall, pupils must not run, romp, or eat, and must take a seat at once and stay in it. Talk stays gentle, and singers gather in the center sections without being asked. A chapter on introductions warns against sloppy forms like Mrs. Jones, meet Miss Holbrook. Dance rules follow, down to the inches between partners and the place of each hand. The book drills courtesy as a habit, not a show.
16355-combed-out:
F. A. V.'s Combed Out, published in London by the Swarthmore Press in 1920, records a soldier's First World War in ten chapters. Squad drill opens the book, with a contemptuous sergeant teaching turns by common sense and exact obedience. The fatigue party, detachment, casualty clearing station, walking wounded, air raids, the German push, home on leave, across the ridges, and the armistice follow.

A Mark Twain epigraph on the national lie that supports tyrannies and shams sets the book's angry, honest tone. The author writes as a ranker, not an officer, about drill, wounds, and waiting. Readers of war memoirs will find a blunt, humane voice from the Western Front.
17412-the-bobbsey-twins-or-merry-days-in:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this first Bobbsey Twins book, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with the subtitle Merry Days Indoors and Out. The twins at home open the story, followed by rope jumping and what followed, the first snow storm, the broken window, and Bert's ghost. Coasting and what came of it, a snow house built by Freddie and Flossie, fun on the ice, and Freddie losing himself complete the early chapters.

Readers get a gentle family story of two sets of twins at play through the seasons, told in Hope's plain, kindly style. The book launched a series that kept children reading for decades. It suits young readers who enjoy everyday adventures, snow, and family fun.
17575-how-to-camp-out:
John M. Gould, author of a history of the First-Tenth-Twenty-Ninth Maine Regiment, wrote this guide to camping, first published in 1877, under the heading Hints for Camping and Walking. The contents open with getting ready, the first of many practical chapters for walkers and campers. Gould writes from experience, not from theory.

Readers learn how to choose ground, pitch camp, cook, walk, and stay safe outdoors, in the plain style of a veteran instructor. The book belongs to the early literature of American outdoor recreation, when camping was becoming a pastime rather than a necessity. It still reads as a sensible, old-fashioned manual for the woods.
1832-the-case-of-the-lamp-that-went-out:
Joseph Muller is no Holmes and no Lecoq: small, slight, plain-looking, and modest in manner, he solves his cases by patience and by noticing what louder men miss. Small, slight, and plain-looking, he works patiently and modestly, noticing what louder men miss.

The case turns on a lamp that went out and on a remark Muller himself recognizes as out of place, almost an impertinence, addressed to a man named Bormann. Groner builds the mystery from small social slips rather than from grand clues. The book is a good sample of the quieter European detective story, where character does the work of fingerprints.
18950-the-short-cut:
Jackson Gregory published this western novel in 1916, illustrated by Frank Tenney Johnson. The chapter titles trace a story of tragedy, suspicion, and pursuit: a homecoming, a gambler's bluff, a contemptuous rival named Sledge Hume, and a woman named Wanda whose discovery changes the game. A figure called Red Reckless and a promise made to little Saxon add to the tangle.

The action moves through ranch houses, town streets, and open country as old wrongs surface and new alliances form. Gregory builds his plot on secrets, grudges, and sudden reversals rather than on gunplay alone. Readers get a romantic western of the old magazine school, with strong heroines, proud villains, and a hero caught between duty and desire.
19501-the-boy-scout:
Richard Harding Davis wrote this story of a boy scout; its New York printing appeared in the mid nineteen teens with pictures. Jimmie, the hero of the frontispiece, drops a valise, straightens cramped fingers, and salutes, a small act that sums up the scout spirit.

Later a head clerk hides tickets in his waistcoat, trembling with excitement over a month-long boat trip in cabins called the Royal Suite. Davis's tale mixes city comedy with scout ideals: readiness, courtesy, and help given without fuss. A white-haired young man in a fast racing car tries to outrun the urge to do a stranger a good turn.
20104-the-cross-cut:
Courtney Ryley Cooper published The Cross-Cut in 1921, a western novel of mines and sudden death. Robert Fairchild finds an old man dead in a big armchair by the windows. A book lies on the worn carpet where it fell from slack hands. Fairchild picks it up and puts it back in the oak case.

That quiet, grim scene opens a tale of claims and cross-cut tunnels. Mining terms and greed shape the fights that follow underground. Cooper knew the West and its camps from his own reporting years. Readers get a tense tale where wealth in rock breeds risk above ground too.
23588-a-filbert-is-a-nut:
Rick Raphael wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in November nineteen fifty nine. It opens with a joke that proves serious: the man in question was a nut, an institutionalised patient nutty enough to think he could build an atom bomb from modelling clay.

Miss Abercrombie, a manual therapist, pats old Mr. Lieberman on the shoulder and praises his finger painting. Patients work at long tables in a hospital arts and crafts shop, watched by bored attendants in spotless whites by a locked door. Raphael builds from that ward to a sharp, humane twist on madness, genius, and what counts as sane. Readers who like wry science fiction will enjoy the tale's blend of hospital detail and atomic dread.
2371-the-filigree-ball-being-a-full-and-:
Anna Katharine Green's Filigree Ball is a detective novel. A young woman is found dead at a ball, clutching a strange filigree ornament, and a lady detective must untangle the case. Green, a pioneer of American mystery fiction, builds the plot from clues, suspects, and a secret marriage, with her usual care for legal and domestic detail. The ballroom setting gives the murder its glitter.

The novel shows Green's gift for fair-play detection before the genre had rules. Its heroine detective was a novelty in her time. Mystery fans will enjoy a classic from the genre's early years.
23871-a-little-union-scout:
Joel Chandler Harris published A Little Union Scout in 1904, with pictures by George Gibbs. Its frame is a young lady, just returned from college, hunting her house for old things: furniture, china, and books. Her craze for the antique leads her to an old scrap-book her mother and the narrator thought safe under lock and key.

Reading it page by page in a sunny place, her curiosity wakes. The clippings tell of Civil War adventures. The illustrations catch their moments: Forrest shouting across a field, Whistling Jim running head down like a bull, and a leader with an evil-looking eye. Harris tells a Union scout's story through a daughter's discovery, with the war's melody wild and melancholy.
23924-kiddie-the-scout:
Robert Leighton published Kiddie the Scout in London in 1920, a continuation of Kiddie of the Camp, inscribed to Bernard Everett, who suggested it. Kiddie, a boy scout of the plains, faces a mysterious sniper, a dangerous enemy, and the sign of the broken feather.

Chapters follow lessons in tracking, a moonlight visitor, and Lone Wolf Cañon, with the cry of the jay and the ruse of the buffalo trail. Rube Carter's theory meets Kiddie's own, evidence mounts for the prosecution, and the battle of Poison Spider Creek settles matters. Leighton, who also wrote Rattlesnake Ranch and Cooee, gives young readers a Western scout story full of trails, clues, and pluck.
2484-the-boys-and-girls-plutarch-being-p:
Plutarch's Lives, retold for boys and girls, brings the great Greeks and Romans to young readers: Alexander and Caesar, Lycurgus and Numa, heroes and lawgivers whose choices shaped the ancient world. The retelling keeps Plutarch's moral focus, asking what made a life great or ruined it. The stories are short, vivid, and full of incident.

The volume served generations as a first history book, teaching character through example. Modern readers will find its heroes simplified but its stories still stirring. It remains a fine introduction to the classical world. The retelling pairs Greek and Roman lives, as Plutarch himself did.
3035-the-day-of-the-confederacy-a-chroni:
Nathaniel Stephenson wrote The Day of the Confederacy, volume thirty of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters follow the secession movement, the Davis government, and the fall of King Cotton. Reaction against Richmond, the critical year, life in the Confederacy, the turning of the tide, a game of chance, and desperate remedies follow. Stephenson writes from the southern side of the war. The book stresses that the Confederacy split into separate units as early as Farragut's capture of New Orleans.

Virginia, the two Carolinas, and Georgia formed the effective system while a detached western world fought alone. The narrative balances politics, economics, and daily life. It gives readers the companion to Stephenson's Union volume, compact and readable.
3538-the-americanization-of-edward-bok-t:
Edward William Bok tells how a Dutch immigrant boy became one of America's most famous magazine editors in this autobiography. Bok, born in 1863, dedicates the book to his mother and his wife, the two women he credits most. He planned to write it in 1914, when he hoped to retire from editing The Ladies' Home Journal, but war delayed the work.

The story follows Bok from a poor immigrant home through newspaper offices to the editorship that shaped American homes. He writes about his own two personalities, the public editor and the private man, and about learning American ways without losing his past. The book won the Pulitzer Prize and suits readers who enjoy immigrant success stories and magazine history.
4525-the-farm-that-won-t-wear-out:
Cyril G. Hopkins first published this farming book in serial form in The Country Gentleman, then issued it in book form after requests from farmers across the central, eastern, and southern states. His argument is plain: a farm need not wear out if its soil is fed and kept fertile year after year. Population growth, he says, makes the art of getting a good living from a small area of soil more valuable than ever.

Chapters take up permanent fertility, the nitrogen problem and its low-cost answer, phosphorus as the master key to lasting farming, and the link between soil care, profits, and future value. Hopkins quotes Lincoln and Liebig to stress that wealth lies in what the soil holds for plants, not in the land alone. Readers get a practical, hopeful manual for farmers who want land that keeps paying, rather than land that slowly fails.
475-in-darkest-england-and-the-way-out:
William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army, sets out his plan to rescue the destitute of Victorian England, which he calls darkest England. Tales of hunger, drink, and homelessness frame a practical scheme. Booth borrowed Stanley's Darkest Africa title to shock readers about London poverty.

Booth proposes colonies, workshops, and farms where the poor could work their way back to honest life, under the Army's care. The book stirred wide debate, and it marks the moment when charity began to speak the language of social reform. His city colonies, farm colonies, and overseas colonies formed a ladder out of destitution.
6636-hold-up-your-heads-girls-helps-for-:
Annie Ryder speaks straight to girls everywhere, with a title borrowed from Whittier's Primrose: hold up your heads, girls. Her chapters teach how to talk, how to know nature, how to make the most of work, what to study, and how to face moods and friends. School and home life both get practical, kind counsel.

Ryder opens with a craftsman's warning: one false stroke near the end can spoil a fine work, just as one careless act can mar a young life. Her tone is warm, not scolding, and her aim is steady character. Hold Up Your Heads, Girls is a charming 1886 conduct book, full of sense for young readers of any age.
6697-once-upon-a-time-in-connecticut:
Caroline Clifford Newton writes Connecticut history for the school children of the state, under the Colonial Dames of America. Yale's Charles Andrews oversaw the history, while friends, libraries, and the Connecticut Historical Society aided the work. The dedication speaks straight to young readers, as the book's true audience.

Tales of early Connecticut follow, told in a clear, story-like style that suits a classroom. The book aims to make state history feel like a tale, not a lesson. Once Upon a Time in Connecticut is a pleasant, old-style children's history, rooted in real places and people.
7436-the-development-of-religious-libert:
M. Louise Greene, who took her doctorate at Yale, traces how Connecticut moved from an established church to religious liberty. The monograph grew from three earlier essays. The first was a Yale thesis on church and state in Connecticut to 1818. The second was a popular article that won the Straus prize in 1896. The third was a paper honored by the American Historical Association in 1901.

The story runs from the colonial order, in which the Congregational church stood established by law, through dissent, taxation disputes, and the constitutional settlement of 1818. Greene argues that the past should teach the present, and that one generation can judge its own beliefs better by studying those of the last. The book is a careful state history with a national lesson about church and state.
8467-frost-s-laws-and-by-laws-of-america:
Frost's Laws and By-Laws of American Society promises a condensed but thorough treatise on etiquette and its usages in America, with plain and reliable directions for deportment in every situation in life. Subjects include letters of introduction, salutes and salutations, calls, conversation, invitations, dinner company, balls, morning and evening parties, visiting, and street etiquette.

S. A. Frost's manual served a rising middle class eager to behave correctly, and its plain directions show what counted as polite in Gilded Age America. Readers today get both a rule book and social history: riding and driving, travelling, and table manners as a system. The book's thoroughness is its charm, and its window onto manners.
9295-a-night-out:
Edward Peple wrote this comic tale in which the hero is a cat, Omar Ben Sufi, a splendid tiger-marked Persian of purest breed. Omar's pedigree runs to Padisha Zim Yuki Yowsi Zind, and his tail rivals Solomon in all his glory. To laymen he was just a cat, dwelling with an exclusive family in an eighty-thousand-dollar cottage near town.

A night out sends Omar into scrapes that wound his aristocratic pride and test his languor. Peple writes with arch humor, letting the cat's dignity carry the jest. The book is a light, charming fancy for animal lovers and humor readers alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beirut:
Beirut, in Phoenicia, is a titular Latin see and the residential see of several Oriental prelates. Its earliest form was likely Beeroth, springs, and Berytos probably comes from Berûti, a fish-goddess's Phoenician name. Birthplace of the early Phoenician author Sanchoniathon, it seems unimportant in remote times. After Antiochus IV Epiphanes it was called Laodicea of Chanaan until Alexander Zabinas (129-123 BC).

Strabo says Tryphon destroyed it, yet its coin series runs complete from 123 to 14 BC, so it was quickly rebuilt. Rome enlarged it, garrisoned it with two legions, and made it the colony Julia Augusta Felix Berytus in 14 BC. Herod the Great and both Agrippas built sumptuous monuments there and gave gladiatorial combats. Its missionaries remain Catholicism's strongest bulwark in Syria, served by a precious documents collection begun at Paris in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-connecticut:
James Henry Webb's entry surveys Connecticut, five thousand square miles. It ranked among the thirteen colonies declaring independence in 1776, early to ratify the Constitution, under which the republic took present form in 1789. The 1900 census counted 908,420 people, passing one million by 1908, growth in cities while rural towns held on. Manufacturing, not farming or commerce, formed the principal resource.

Plymouth traders founded the first English settlement at Windsor in 1633. Dutch traders raised a house and fort upriver. Windsor, Hartford, and Wethersfield united on 24 January 1639 under a first constitution. Connecticut ceded public lands in 1786, reserving some three and a half million Ohio acres, and adopted its present constitution in 1818. Religious polity runs through the entry. Puritan planters framed the 1639 constitution. Sunday observance stood strictly by law, blasphemy statutes dated from settlement, and Assembly sessions opened with prayer and chaplains. Statutes regulated church societies and incorporation, while confessional communications carried no legal privilege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-greyso:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Greysolon, Sieur du Lhut, the French explorer who gave Duluth its name. Born near Saint-Germain-Laval about 1640 and dead at Montreal in 1710, he served in the French army, fought at Senef in 1674, and sailed for Canada that same year.

From Montreal he pushed west in 1678. He took possession of the Sioux country for France in 1679. He explored Lake Superior and the high plateau where the Mississippi, Red, and Saint Lawrence rivers rise. He built Kaministiquia, now Fort William, and Fort La Tourette on Lake Nepigon. First Canadian to explore the West, he rescued Father Hennepin from captivity and laid the foundation of Detroit in 1686.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-father-prout:
Father Prout was the pen name of Francis Sylvester Mahony, Irish priest and writer. Born at Cork in 1804, he studied at Clongowes and in France. Ordained at Lucca in 1832 against his superiors' advice, he served in Cork. During the cholera epidemic he worked heroically as a hospital chaplain.

Moving to London in 1834, Mahony began writing for Fraser's Magazine. Dickens later posted him to Rome for the Daily News. His Reliques of Father Prout mix erudition, fancy, and sharp and caustic wit. Best known for The Bells of Shandon, he died in Paris in 1866.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-cabassut:
Jean Cabassut, a French Oratorian theologian born at Aix in 1604 and dead there in 1685, joined learning to holiness and a ready charity. He entered the Oratory at twenty-one, taught canon law at Avignon, and spent eighteen months at Rome with Cardinal Grimaldi, archbishop of Aix.

Back home Cabassut wrote on church history, canon law, and moral theology, and Saint Alphonsus counted him a classic. His Notice of Councils, enlarged in 1680 into a collated history of councils and canons, long served as an authority under the name Cabassutius. His canon law theory and practice ran through many editions across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-amadeu:
Johann Amadeus Franz de Paula Thugut, an Austrian statesman born at Linz in 1736 and died at Vienna in 1818. He was a paymaster's son called Franz through life, despite the baptismal Johann Amadeus. Tales of Maria Theresa finding him abandoned are myths; she schooled him at the new Oriental academy for his father's service.

Thugut entered imperial service in 1754 as translator at Constantinople, won Kaunitz's praise, and became state chancery secretary. All the while he secretly drawing thirteen thousand livres a year from Louis XV, a pension he kept as embassy secretary from 1769. Raised to lower nobility in 1771, he later persuaded the Turks on Bukovina and steered Austrian policy through revolution and war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kharput:
Kharput, Armenian Kharpert, meaning 'rocky fortress', is an Armenian Catholic diocese founded in 1850 in eastern Anatolia. This entry describes a very old hill city, built under the first Armenian kings, whose ruined fortress, tower, and walls still stand at about 4,350 feet.

Height and scarce water are pushing residents down to Mezre, three miles away on the plain. Kharput still holds 30,000 people and serves as capital of the newly created province (vilayet) of Mamouret-ul-Aziz. The diocese counts 3,000 faithful, eight parishes, six churches, three chapels, 14 stations, and 14 primary schools. Some 72,000 Christians live among about 600,000 people in the whole province. An American Protestant mission, large and based at Kharput, heads all such missions in Armenia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-wolge:
Michael Wolgemut, a painter and engraver, was born at Nuremberg in 1434 and died there in 1519. He stood as Nuremberg's foremost fifteenth-century artist, picked to paint the great altarpiece at Zwickau. Hans Pleydenwurff had him as pupil and helper; Wolgemut took over his master's technique with care, though he must not be ranked his equal. His surest claim to lasting fame is that Durer learned from him, working alongside him from 1486 to 1490.

In those years his workshop counted among the city's busiest, crowded, Dodgson notes, by the best painters, carvers, and wood engravers of the day. Whether Wolgemut cut wood himself is still unsettled, but many carved wooden altarpieces came out of his shop, and Veit Stoss, the famed carver, was his friend and workmate. He plainly made some woodcuts, and designs for several Nuremberg stained-glass windows are his. His chief picture after the Zwickau one hangs at Crailsheim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-denaut:
Pierre Denaut was the tenth Bishop of Quebec, born at Montreal on 20 July 1743. Schooled at Montreal and Quebec, he was ordained in 1767 and made pastor of Soulanges at only twenty-four. During the American invasion of 1775 he kept his flock faithful to their sovereign. Transferred to Longueuil in 1787 and made vicar-general in 1791, he became coadjutor to Bishop Hubert and was consecrated on 29 June 1795.

He stayed at Longueuil after succeeding to Quebec in 1797, governing chiefly with Bishop Plessis. He visited his whole diocese, crossing Upper Canada to Detroit in 1801 and 1802. In 1803, via Burlington and Boston, he reached the Maritime Provinces, where Acadians and Indians saw a bishop for the first time. He founded Nicolet College in 1803 and helped enlarge Montreal College in 1804. He resisted a British governor's claim to present to parishes and the Royal Institution's Protestant control of instruction. He died at Longueuil in 1806.
doe-osti-2997324-an-assessment-of-the-er: WIPP porosity errors got assessed, and this DOE report covers the response surface computation. The pages detail the error analysis. The repository modelers get their numbers. The plant was Waste Isolation Pilot. The surface was porosity response. The modelers got numbers.
doe-osti-3007880-a-north-carolina-retros: North Carolina outages got retrospectived, and this DOE text trends Helene with TASTI-GRID. The pages detail the major findings. The grid folks get their briefing. The hurricane was Helene. The briefing was grid. The trends were outage. The grid was TASTI.
doe-osti-3007891-cleap-project-or-sage-a: CLEAP got its OR-SAGE analysis, and this DOE project covers MT, UT, CO states. The pages detail the findings. The planners get their numbers. The states were Montana, Utah, Colorado. The numbers were planner. The project was CLEAP. The states were western.
doe-osti-3009942-reticular-materials-and: Seawater mining got AI-simulated, and this DOE final covers reticular materials. The pages detail the metal findings. The chemists get their closeout. The metals were valuable. The closeout was chemist. The mining was seawater. The simulations were computer. The metals were mined.
doe-osti-3023487-participation-in-intens: Neutrino physics got intensity-participated, and this DOE closeout reports the frontier. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their closeout. The report was closeout. The closeout was physicist. The frontier was intensity. The physics was neutrino. The closeout was report.
doe-osti-3030267-bull-trout-and-westslop: Trout got tailrace-tracked, and this DOE text follows bull and cutthroat. The pages detail the dam findings. The environmental folks get their data. The movement was tailrace. The data were environmental. The cutthroat were westslope. The tailrace were dam.
doe-osti-3366851-potential-applications-: Quantum computing got LANL-applied, and this DOE v0.3.0 covers potential uses. The pages detail the applications findings. The quantum folks get their data. The laboratory was Los Alamos. The data were quantum. The v0.3.0 were applications. The Alamos were Los.
doe-osti-3484507-energy-storage-siting-a: Storage siting got workshop-reported, and this DOE report covers permitting outreach. The pages detail the energy findings. The energy folks get their data. The workshop was outreach. The data were energy. The outreach were report. The siting were storage.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAUnitedAutoWo:
The headline carries the whole story of a 1967 embarrassment: Ex-Agent Says Victor Made Request; Reuther Concedes UAW Got CIA Funds. Frank C. Porter reported for the Washington Post on the United Auto Workers' turn in the great CIA funding scandal.

When the agency's secret subsidies to private organizations broke into print, labor's turn came. An ex-agent said Victor Reuther had requested the money, and Walter Reuther conceded the union had received CIA funds for its international work. The article is one clipping from the avalanche that ended the CIA's covert funding of American civic life. It is preserved as it ran.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RayJerryAbout_R: FBI agents interviewed Jerry William Ray on April 29, 1968, three weeks after the King assassination. Jerry Ray was James Earl Ray's brother, and agents questioned the family hard in the manhunt's last weeks. An interview record fixes the date, the place in the inquiry, and the man's own statements as agents wrote them down. The file gives the interview's date and subject. It does not summarize Jerry Ray's answers, so they cannot be described here.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Ins: Able Archer 83 was a NATO exercise in November 1983 that rehearsed the release of nuclear weapons. Soviet leaders, fearing the drill might mask a real attack, put their own forces on alert. This briefing-book page presents the record of that war game and the scare around it. Its title says the episode put United States-Soviet relations on a hair trigger. The evidence here is the title alone, but the event is now widely treated as one of the Cold War's most dangerous misunderstandings.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico-a: Keeping the Secrets: US Silence about Ayotzinapa - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
hold-up-your-heads-girls-helps-for-girls:
Annie H. Ryder's Hold Up Your Heads, Girls! offers practical help for girls in school and out of it. Ryder borrows her title from Whittier's Primrose, who told her daughters that handsome conduct, not looks, is what counts. She dedicates the book to her girls everywhere.

Chapters advise on how to talk, how to get acquainted with nature, and how to make the most of work. They also discuss what to study, and how English literature and other studies fit a young woman's education. Later chapters treat moods, womanliness, friendship and the relations of youths and maidens, always in a direct, encouraging tone. The book speaks to readers who want a period picture of how a thoughtful Victorian author counselled girls toward confident, useful lives.
in-darkest-england-and-the-way-out:
General William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army, published In Darkest England and the Way Out in 1890 as a plan to rescue Britain's poorest. Part one, The Darkness, counts what Booth called the submerged tenth: the homeless, the out-of-work, drunkards, criminals, and children of the lost. He piles up cases and figures from London streets.

Part two, Deliverance, lays out his scheme in detail. City colonies would feed and employ men, farm colonies retrain them, and a colony overseas would settle them abroad. Rescue homes, a prison-gate brigade, a poor man's bank, and a poor man's lawyer complete the design. Booth wrote as an organizer raising an army, not a bystander.
layamon-s-brut:
Layamon's Brut is an early English poem retelling Britain's legendary history. The hosted sample opens in the thick of battle and march. Constantin the Fair lands at Totnes with all his host.

Two thousand knights march with him toward London. The Britons hide in pits, woods, heaths, and fens to escape. Messengers summon every brave man in the kingdom to court. Layamon wrote in English soon after the Norman age. His poem preserves old British tales in a rough, powerful early verse. Arthur stands at the center of Layamon's long chronicle. Battles and kings pass in a stately, drum-like rhythm.
manners-and-conduct-in-school-and-out:
Manners and Conduct in School and Out was written by the deans of girls in Chicago high schools. Allyn and Bacon published it, copyrighted in 1921 by Fanny R. Smith. A line from Spenser opens it: the gentle mind is known by gentle deeds. Maxims from Lincoln, Franklin, and Disraeli follow.

The book teaches schoolgirls how to act in class and beyond it. Lessons cover speech, dress, honesty, and respect for others. Its sayings urge that whatever is worth doing is worth doing well. Time, warns Franklin, is the stuff life is made of. Such manuals shaped American school manners for a generation. This one speaks with the voice of women educators.
nasa-tm-19690017085-manned-space-station:
Robert R. Gilruth, director of the Manned Spacecraft Center, presented this speech in San Antonio on June 25, 1968. He spoke at the Fourth International Symposium on Bioastronautics and the Exploration of Space. His theme is the manned space station as gateway to our future in space. That old dream of engineers, he argues, is newly practical.

Three developments clarified the picture, Gilruth says. The Saturn V rocket now provides a major building block for station design. Knowledge of the living and working environment crews need has also grown greatly. Station science programs, studied in depth, now define real use requirements. He closes with present Apollo Applications plans and speculations on future orbital stations.
once-upon-a-time-in-connecticut:
Caroline Clifford Newton wrote these tales of early Connecticut. The Colonial Dames of Connecticut sponsored the book. They dedicated it to the school children of the state. Professor Charles Andrews of Yale supervised its history. Libraries and the state historical society helped prepare it.

The introduction praises Connecticut's quiet, steady colonial life. Towns were scattered, rural, and largely self-governing, it says. Roads were poor and travel slow between settlements. Town meetings handled local affairs for ordinary people. The colony shaped men and forms of government, it argues. Children gain a love of their local past here.
people-of-the-whirlpool-from-the-experie:
Mabel Osgood Wright called People of the Whirlpool the experience book of a commuter's wife, and dated it 1903. It takes the form of a journal, opening on February 2, Candlemas, in mild gray weather. The writer jokes that if the woodchuck ventures out and sees no shadow, winter owes them a rebate.

The contents promise twins, Miss Lavinia's letters to Barbara, Martin Cortright's letters, and Barbara's trips to town. The whirlpool is New York society, pulling at a household trying to live in the country. Wright mixes nature notes, gossip, and letters into a commuter-age comedy of manners.
the-americanization-of-edward-bok-the-au:
Edward William Bok, whose dates are given as 1863 to 1930, tells his own life in The Americanization of Edward Bok, subtitled the autobiography of a Dutch boy fifty years after. He dedicates the account to his mother and his wife. One gave him birth and raised him, he says; the other blessed him with home and family.

Bok explains that the book was planned for 1914, when he meant to retire from active editorship, but war brought new duties and set it aside. He chose then to write of himself in the third person. That distance, he says, let him watch the public editor Bok at work, praising and blaming him as if he were another man.
the-bobbsey-twins-or-merry-days-indoors-: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins, or Merry Days Indoors and Out, the first book of her long set. Grosset and Dunlap of New York put it out, with rights dated 1904 from the Mershon Company. The first parts place the twins at home, then take up rope jumping and what came of it. The First Snow Storm, The Broken Window, and Bert's Ghost follow. Coasting, and What Came of It is the last part named. A plate shows two sleds sweeping down a long hill.
the-boy-scout:
Richard Harding Davis wrote The Boy Scout, put out in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1914. The tale opens with the scout rule: each day, do some one a good turn. Davis is clear on the spirit of it. The turn is not done since the copy-books say a kind act earns one back. A true scout, till the act is done, has a dark day.

Once the turn is proved, the scout may face the world with a clear mind and untie the knot in his scarf. Jimmie Reeder unties that knot at ten past eight on a hot August morning. His good turn was to give one dime to his sister Sadie. With it she could go to a show, and the plate shows Jimmie, valise dropped, pulling his cramped fingers straight to salute. Small stakes, warmly told, set the tale's tone.
the-boys-and-girls-plutarch-being-parts-: The Boys' and Girls' Plutarch holds parts of the Lives of Plutarch, edited for boys and girls by John S. White. The list starts with Theseus and Romulus, set side by side, then Lycurgus and Solon. Themistocles, Camillus, Pericles, Demosthenes, and Cicero follow. Alcibiades and Coriolanus are paired, as are Aristides with Cimon. Pompey, Alexander the Great, and The Death of Caesar stand in the list too. Short pieces are cut from other lives, among them the engines of Archimedes and a portrait of Cleopatra.
the-case-of-the-lamp-that-went-out:
The Case of the Lamp That Went Out, by Augusta Groner, translated by Grace Isabel Colbron, begins with the same introduction to Joe Muller used across the Muller volumes. Muller, of the Imperial Austrian secret service, is small, slight, and plain, with none of Sherlock Holmes's authority or Monsieur Lecoq's brilliancy.

His humility has causes. A wrongful imprisonment in his youth left a stigma. It shut him out of honest work until the police took him. The bureaucracy of his department keeps his rank low. Yet kings and councillors consult him. He asks no honours, only an income for his simple needs and the chance to work at what he most enjoys. The detective is fully drawn before his case is allowed to start.
the-day-of-the-confederacy-a-chronicle-o: Nathaniel W. Stephenson wrote The Day of the Confederacy as volume 30 of the Chronicles of America series, edited by Allen Johnson and printed at Yale University Press in 1919. The subtitle calls it a chronicle of the embattled South. Its contents begin with the secession movement, the Davis government, the fall of King Cotton, and reaction against Richmond. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here.
the-development-of-religious-liberty-in-:
M. Louise Greene, PhD, explains in a preface that her monograph on religious liberty in Connecticut grew from three earlier, shorter essays. The first, Church and State in Connecticut to 1818, was her doctor's thesis at Yale. The second won the Straus prize offered in 1896 through Brown University by the Hon. Oscar S. Straus, and the third took honorable mention in the Justin Winsor prize competition of 1901.

Connecticut's path, she argues, was not marked by wild disorder, cruel oppression, class tyranny, or civil war. Its contribution was a pattern of stability and reason in government, slowly broadening the idea of liberty as restrictions on religious and personal freedom softened. Yet New England is recalled as a hard place for those who were not Congregationalists, and she hopes a fairer judgment of colonial men and measures will follow.
the-farm-that-won-t-wear-out:
Cyril G. Hopkins wrote The Farm That Won't Wear Out first as a series in The Country Gentleman, then as a book at the call of farmers in many states. Words from Lincoln and from Liebig head the work.

Hopkins asks what makes soil stay rich for good. His chapters take up what crops take out of land, the puzzle of nitrogen and its cheap fix, and phosphorus, which he calls the master key to lasting farming. He ties soil wealth to farm profit and land value. The aim is plain: feed the soil so a farm can feed folk for good.
the-filigree-ball-being-a-full-and-true-:
Anna Katharine Green wrote The Filigree Ball as a mystery in three books, from The Forbidden Room to The House of Doom. A full and true account of a crime's solution is promised on the title line.

The first book opens with talk of the Moore house, a signed name, Veronica, and gossip at work. The second book turns to law and its victim, with thrust and parry in court. The third moves south to Tampa and a colonel's own men, seeking the heart of the puzzle. Green builds her case from small clues, house secrets, and a ball where a fine chain holds the key.
the-short-cut: Jackson Gregory wrote The Short Cut, published by Dodd, Mead and Company in New York in 1916. Frank Tenney Johnson supplied the illustrations. He dedicated the book to Mother McGlashan and General C. F. McGlashan. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents only. The tragedy opens the list of chapters. The shadow, suspicion, and the white huntress follow. Red Reckless comes home at chapter five. Wanda's discovery is promised at chapter eleven, where the shown list ends.
the-voyage-out: Woolf's 1915 Voyage Out sends Rachel to South America and awakening. Her first novel. The Tower library holds the full text. It sailed outward. Youth woke. Love stirred. Death came. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
